Batch and Stream ProcessingBatch processes a bounded set; streaming updates results as more events arrive

The difference is how ongoing input becomes an updated result

The Same Readings, Different UpdatesThe same count can be computed after a batch or updated during a stream

Streaming makes a current result available before the input stops

Four Readings from One MachineEach row is one M1 reading; count readings at or above 80°C

ReadingMeasured atArrived atTemperature
E110:0110:0182°C
E210:0410:0486°C
E310:0610:0690°C
E410:0310:0784°C
E4 describes an earlier measurement that arrives last

Snapshots and Event StreamsA current value answers “what is it now?”; events preserve how it changed

A snapshot keeps one state; an event stream preserves individual changes

One Event, One ReadingAn event records one occurrence with its own identity

FieldE1 valueMeaning
event_idE1This measurement
machine_idM1The machine
measured_at10:01When it happened
temperature82°CThe measured value
E1 identifies the reading; M1 identifies its machine

The First Record in a LogA log appends incoming events in order

E1 occupies position 0 in the stored log

New Readings Append at the End

E1 remains stored when E2 and E3 append

A Late Reading Still Appends Last

E4 receives position 3 even though it happened before E3

Producer, Log and ConsumerThe producer writes events; the consumer reads them

Writing a reading and processing its result are separate steps

LinkedIn Needed Fresh Activity DataActivity logs became inputs to live services as well as later analysis

The same event data had to reach both live services and batch analysis

Kafka Begins at LinkedInKafka was open-sourced in 2011 to deliver activity records to online and offline systems

A shared log connected the activity producers to different readers

Kafka Holds the Event Log

The topic gives the event stream a name

Kafka ConsumersThe broker stores events; a consumer turns them into a useful result

The reports and dashboards are downstream of the consumer

Decoupling Writers and ReadersA retained log lets writers and readers work at different times

A new reader can use the log without adding a new producer connection

Two Readers, Two PositionsIndependent readers can consume the same retained events at their own pace

The display resumes at E4; the report resumes at E2

Partitions Split a Topic into LogsA partition is one ordered log; separate partitions have separate positions

Each partition has its own sequence and its own next offset

A Key Keeps One Machine TogetherHere the record key is the machine ID

The fixed mapping sends every M1 reading to the same log

Partition Order and Event TimeKeeping a machine together preserves its log order, even when measurement times arrive out of order

M1 stays in one partition, yet E4 still arrives after E3

An Offset Names a PositionOffsets belong to one partition

PartitionOffsetStored reading
00E1 from M1
01E2 from M1
10A reading from M2
Offset 0 in two partitions identifies two different records

Consumer GroupsOne group shares the work; separate groups each read the stream

Both groups read all three partitions, with different assignments

Partition Assignment and RebalancingAdding consumers helps only while partitions remain available to assign

Three partitions provide at most three active readers within this group

A Hot Key Limits ThroughputTotal capacity can exceed total input while one partition still falls behind

Partition 0: 900 − 600 = +300 events/s; total input 1,000 < total capacity 1,200
Partition 0 accumulates 300 unread events every second

Lag and Catch-UpCatch-up capacity is the processing rate left after handling new arrivals

Input falls to 300 events/s: 18,000 / (600 − 300) = 60 s
18,000 queued events take 60 seconds to drain at 300 extra events per second

Broker ReplicationCopies on other brokers support recovery; they consume extra storage

10 GB logical data × 3 replicas = 30 GB payload
Three replicas preserve one logical partition, rather than three independent streams

Batching within a StreamAmortizing a request over more records reduces overhead, but adds waiting time

Request cost: (2 ms + 100 × 0.1 ms) / 100 = 0.12 ms per record
The sender groups records by partition before sending them

Reading the First Record

After processing E1, the next read position becomes 1

Reading the Second Record

Two processed readings produce two result rows

Saving the Restart PositionCommitting an offset saves where a reader should resume

Saved position 2 means E3 is the next record after restart

A Failure Before Saving the Position

E3 reaches the result, but saved position remains 2

Restarting from the Saved Position

The restarted reader returns to E3 at offset 2

The Same Reading Can Appear TwiceReplay means reading stored records again

Three distinct readings can produce four rows after replay

Reading ID and Machine ID

Stored inputMachineEvent identity
First measurementM1E1
Second measurementM1E2
E3 replayM1E3 again
Different M1 events survive; a second copy of E3 does not

Keeping One Result Row per Event

A unique event ID keeps replay from adding a second row

Demo: Read, Save and RestartPredict the result after restart, then repeat with unique event IDs

Simulation: read E1 and E2, save position, read E3, restart, then read E3 again

Compare result rows before and after reading E3 a second time

Answer: Read, Save and Restart

ActionSaved positionResult rows
Read E1 and E2; save2E1 E2
Read E3; restart2E1 E2 E3
Read E3 again2E1 E2 E3 E3
Repeat with unique event IDs2E1 E2 E3
The saved position controls replay; event identity controls repeated result rows

Processing Before Saving Progress

Saving progress after the result leaves replay possible during a failure

Failure Windows and DeliveryAt-most-once can lose an effect; at-least-once can repeat one

Write orderCrash between writesOutcome on restart
Save offset → resultOffset advanced; result absentE3 is skipped
Result → save offsetE3 stored; offset unchangedE3 is replayed
Atomic result + progressBoth commit or both roll backConsistent recovery
The failure gap comes from storing the result and progress separately

Deduplication and State UpdatesEvent identity helps only when deduplication and the effect recover together

An existing event ID must prevent both another row and another increment

Rebuilding a Result from the Log

A retained log can rebuild a result from the same input

Kafka Connect and Stream ProcessingConnect moves records between systems; a stream application computes results

Ingestion, stateful computation and output are different responsibilities

Handling Late Arrivals

use the measurement time to update the right result

One Reading Has Two TimesEvent time is when the measurement happened

E4 happened at 10:03 and arrived at 10:07

Counting by Measurement TimeCount hot readings in each five-minute measurement interval

Before E4 arrives, the earlier interval contains E1 and E2

A Late Arrival Updates the Earlier Interval

E4 changes the earlier count from 2 to 3

The Clock Changes the Answer

Time used10:00 to before 10:0510:05 to before 10:10
Measurement timeE1 E2 E4: 3E3: 1
Arrival timeE1 E2: 2E3 E4: 2
Measurement time and arrival time answer different questions

Replacing the Earlier Result

The revised count replaces 2 with 3 for the same interval

Watermarks and Window ClosureA watermark expresses progress in event time; closing a window commits to a lateness policy

With zero delay allowance, E3 closes the earlier window before E4 arrives

Waiting for Late EventsA larger allowance keeps state longer and permits later corrections

A two-minute allowance keeps the earlier window open for E4

Demo: Delay and Window ClosureChange arrival time and delay allowance independently

Single input: watermark = maximum observed event time − delay allowance; close at 10:05

Compare early arrival, late rejection and a retained correction

Answer: Delay and Window ClosureThe same four events produce different accepted results under different closure policies

E4 arrivesDelay allowanceEarlier countWindow after E3
10:070 min2; E4 droppedClosed
10:072 min3; E4 includedOpen
10:030 min3; E4 includedClosed
Waiting longer changes acceptance; earlier arrival avoids the closure gap

Window State and RetentionKeeping more windows supports corrections but increases retained state

1,000 keys × 3 windows × (8-byte count + 8-byte sum) = 48,000 bytes
Doubling active windows doubles this aggregate payload from 48,000 to 96,000 bytes

Takeaway: Stream Processing

1Partitions set ordering and parallelism; hot keys can dominate lag
2Recovery joins durable progress with replay-safe effects
3Event time sets window membership; lateness policy sets closure
